title: Where it worked
hook: where did Stoic practice actually change a day?

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Arethas, the bishop who kept a worn copy of Marcus's notebook. Your line was to himself, to us.

What would count as evidence? A runner can show a race time. A baker can show the bread. A year of Stoic reading has no scoreboard. Its evidence is quieter: a sharp remark someone didn't make, a night someone slept instead of rehearsing an argument, a loss met a little more steadily. Nobody hands out medals for those, and they're easy to forget by the weekend. So today is for looking, on purpose, one at a time. Where did it actually work?
screen: `NO SCOREBOARD FOR THIS.` → `A SHARP REMARK, NOT MADE.` → `WHERE DID IT ACTUALLY WORK?`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics' own test. Epictetus was blunt about where progress shows. Not in how many books you've read, he says in the Discourses, but in what you do with your desires and fears, in how you meet the day. In the Handbook he gives a picture: sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they ate. They digest it, and give wool and milk. So the question isn't what you know about Stoicism. It's where the wool showed. Second, the evidence is small. Look back down the year at the tools: a reply delayed, from Stoic in anger. A worry sorted into two columns, from Stoic at work. The evening questions, asked kindly. The view from above, for a night when something feels enormous. These are tiny hinges. A door swings on them anyway. Third, be specific. A vague sense that it helped won't hold up on a hard day. A real moment will: a time, a place, what you would have done, what you did instead. Marcus wrote book one that way: not my teachers were good, but from this one person, this one thing. Fourth, the week behind you: three habits to keep, one idea to leave, the first page reread, and thanks to a freed slave, a flawed courtier, and an emperor who wrote to himself. Today is for the proof, in your own life, that any of it mattered. Tomorrow, just as honestly, the other side.
screen: `THE TEST: WHERE THE WOOL SHOWED.` · `SMALL HINGES SWING BIG DOORS.` · `A TIME, A PLACE, A CHOICE.` · `A WEEK OF KEEPING AND THANKS.` · then, large: `IT WORKED HERE.`

segments.voice: Let the year scroll back slowly, looking not for a big transformation but for one moment: a reply you held back, a worry you set down, a morning that began with an intention instead of your phone. When one comes, stay with it: where were you, what would you have done before, and what did you do? If nothing comes, that's worth knowing too.
Discourses, Epictetus's teaching where progress shows not in books read but in a reply delayed, a worry sorted, a moment met well. Today's word.
Your line: it worked here. If someone asks what a year of this gave you, that moment is your answer. That's day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a journal and note specific moments when a principle changed what they did, as evidence of progress rather than knowledge.

fork.setup: a friend asks what a year of Stoic practice actually did for you. what do you say?
options: I can explain the dichotomy of control
one specific moment I did something differently

fork.reveal: Epictetus would want the wool, not the grass: a real moment where it changed what you did.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoicism works if you feel calm all the time.
what it means: it worked in particular moments, a reply delayed, a worry set down, and you can name them.

what a scholar hears: Epictetus places progress in the work itself, in desire, aversion and action (Discourses 1.4), and Handbook 46 pictures it as sheep giving wool and milk instead of showing their grass.

chat.says: So after a year of Stoic reading, how do you know it actually worked?
options: Look for small, specific moments, like a reply held back, not books read.
If you can quote the key lines from memory, then it's working.
If people around you start calling you a Stoic, it's worked.
chat.meaning: Epictetus says progress shows not in books read but in how you meet the day, like sheep giving wool, not showing grass.
